summary: Weekly sync focused on stability after recent kernel upgrade attempt; customer reported intermittent egress errors and higher p99 latency during bursts. Discussed rollforward plan (kernel 2.4 canary), telemetry gaps, MTU and BGP causes, and next steps to run a 12-hr soak and a security deep-dive. Agreement to collect packet captures and to test with continuous batching disabled briefly to isolate KV cache behavior.
topics: Kernel canary rollout and rollback criteria
P99 latency during bursts and KV cache warmup
Telemetry and audit logs for Private deployment
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (AsterMed Platform), Liam O'Connor (AsterMed MLOps), Sara Weber (AsterMed Security), Tomáš Novak (AsterMed NetOps)

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, um, quick agenda—stability update, kernel canary plan, telemetry gaps and then actions. Diego, want to start with what we saw overnight?

[00:18] Diego Ramos: yeah, sure. So this morning the canary we pushed to the staging onprem cluster hit a p99 spike during a burst test. The median looked fine but the 99, and sometimes 99.9, jumped. We think it's correlated with node egress retries when the batcher backpressures, so there's a coupling between continuous batching and the KV cache warmup behavior.

[00:40] Priya Singh: to be clear, that was after the 2.3 -> 2.4 kernel bump? Because our patch notes show that, but, uh, original patch was intended to resolve a NIC driver stall.

[00:50] Diego Ramos: correct, this was kernel 2.4 canary. The driver change mitigates stalls under heavy VRF egress, but it also changed NIC ring timing a bit — so MTU boundary conditions pop up. We saw occasional path MTU discovery delays.

[01:05] Tomáš Novak: yeah we saw a ton of ICMP fragmentation messages in the netstack; sometimes BGP sessions would flit, not a hard drop but flapping enough to cause re-route. I can share pcap later.

[01:18] Liam O'Connor: to add, when the re-route happened, Redwood's fallback routing kicked in which is good, but the model requests that hit the fallback variant had a 20–30% higher token latency. That's causing user-surface errors in our staging telemetry.

[01:34] Maya Chen: thanks, that's the exact tradeoff we expected — fallback keeps you available but at the cost of both latency and token economics. The goal here is to find the narrow path: fix the networking so you don't hit fallback for normal traffic while still having the fallback as a safety valve.

[01:48] Sara Weber: security question — when fallback triggers, are audit logs preserved and are we still within our KMS encryption boundaries? We need to demonstrate chain-of-custody for SOC2.

[01:57] Diego Ramos: quick answer: yes, logs continue to be written to the private control plane. There was a small telemetry gap we identified where our sidecar didn't forward some early startup traces — we're pushing a patch to ensure immediate buffer flush on failover.

[02:13] Priya Singh: that's the telemetry gap we noticed. Our retention policy requires immutable logs for 90 days; can you confirm the storage location for those failover logs?

[02:22] Maya Chen: we'll share the exact S3/GCS path and the retention policy mapping. Diego, please include the log key prefixes in the artifact list.

[02:31] Diego Ramos: will do. Also adding, during repro we tried two modes: continuous batching enabled vs disabled. With batching disabled the p99 drops significantly, which points to a batching + KV cache warmup interdependency. There's a possible fix in the canary to pre-warm KV cache for pinned models, but it needs testing.

[02:49] Tomáš Novak: pre-warm how? like priming the KV cache on startup? that could increase memory usage but might stabilize latency.

[02:57] Diego Ramos: yep prime at startup for hot routes, with an LRU expiration tuned to your traffic pattern. We can also reduce batch windows to lower tail effects. There's a balance to keep cost in line.

[03:12] Liam O'Connor: cost is important — remember we're metric-ing tokens and infra separately. If pre-warm doubles memory we may overshoot footprint. We prefer less memory and more deterministic latency, but we'll find the right config.

[03:24] Priya Singh: on the MTU thing — we have a legacy edge router doing 1500, but some internal links are 9000 (jumbo). The fragmentation shows when packets traverse mixed MTU paths. Could that explain the odd retries?

[03:36] Diego Ramos: absolutely. If PMTUD is delayed, TCP will retransmit and that shows as increased service latency. For UDP-based health checks and GRPC keepalives it could look like BGP jitter.

[03:46] Sara Weber: aside from SOC2, we have a compliance ask: we need KMS attestations that keys don't leave our HSM when fallback is used — any variance there?

[03:56] Maya Chen: no variance, KMS calls are made from the private control plane locked into your VPC. Diego, we'll include an architecture diagram with SAML/SAML SSO flows and KMS boundary notes.

[04:07] Diego Ramos: noted. I'll add explicit call paths and audit log samples.

[04:12] Maya Chen: ok, let's run through the canary plan and rollback criteria so we're all aligned — Diego?

[04:18] Diego Ramos: Plan A: deploy kernel 2.4 to two canary nodes in the onprem pool (non-critical serving). Enable continuous batching monitoring, and run synthetic burst tests (10k req/min) for 3 hours, then 12-hour soak if no p99 > target and no egress flaps. Rollback criteria: any sustained p99 > 250ms for > 5 minutes, any BGP session error rate above baseline, or any audit/log gap discovered.

[04:42] Priya Singh: what baseline do we use for BGP error rate? Our normal is <0.2% session flaps per hour.

[04:49] Diego Ramos: use your historical as baseline; we'll set an absolute threshold of 0.5% for the canary window to be safe.

[04:55] Tomáš Novak: also, if we see PMTU blackholes, I'd like to enable TCP MSS clamp as a temporary mitigation while we trace path MTU.

[05:03] Diego Ramos: good mitigation, and we'll instrument the flow to detect PMTUD failures.

[05:10] Liam O'Connor: one more thing — during the earlier run, we saw a small burst where the fallback model served older quantized variant which produced a subtle quality regression. We need to tag that as a user-impact event even if latency stayed okay.

[05:22] Maya Chen: understood — we'll add a quality regression flag to the rollback criteria: any change in ROUGE/BLEU or model output distribution above your guardrail. Diego, can Redwood inject a canary variant that maintains output parity?

[05:32] Diego Ramos: yes, we can pin a canary variant that uses the same quantization settings, but the kernel-level NIC timing may still affect token timing. We need to separate quality deltas from timing deltas in telemetry.

[05:44] Priya Singh: telemetry — currently we don't get per-token timing in our logs; we get per-request latencies. Can Redwood add per-token percentiles for the pilot?

[05:54] Diego Ramos: we can enable token-level tracing in the sandbox. It will increase log volume but we can limit windowed traces — e.g., sample 5% of requests during the soak.

[06:05] Sara Weber: and are those token traces encrypted the same way as request logs? we need to ensure PII not leaking.

[06:11] Maya Chen: yes, same KMS boundary. We'll provide a privacy matrix.

[06:16] Speaker 1: okay so next steps from a networking side — Tomáš will push pcaps and BGP logs.

[06:23] Tomáš Novak: I'll drop a tarball to the secure share, and annotate timestamps where we saw flaps. Expect that by tomorrow morning.

[06:30] Priya Singh: question about the continuous batching toggle — you mentioned disabling briefly to isolate KV cache; can we do a traffic-shift test that toggles batching for 15 minutes?

[06:38] Diego Ramos: yes, we can run runbooks that change the global batching window at route level; we'll do a controlled window and compare p99. Also can do a no-batching run for 30 minutes during low-traffic.

[06:48] Maya Chen: good. Diego, add the exact runbook steps to the doc and I'll send to Priya for approval.

[06:54] Diego Ramos: will do.

[07:00] Liam O'Connor: for acceptance criteria — assuming the 12-hour soak passes, what's the recommended rollout cadence? full pool in 48 hours?

[07:07] Diego Ramos: if soak passes with no alerts and p99 within target, we usually do a staggered 25% increment every 4 hours with automated health checks. With your stricter compliance, we can extend to 8-hour windows.

[07:18] Priya Singh: 8 hours sounds safer. Also, we want a dry-run of the rollback to ensure it is fast; can you simulate rollback in staging?

[07:25] Diego Ramos: yes, simulate both a soft rollback (traffic re-route) and hard rollback (package revert). Soft rollback is usually sub-minute; hard rollback depends on your orchestration but we can pre-place the older kernel package to cut time.

[07:40] Maya Chen: switching briefly to security: Sara, you had a list of SOC2 evidence we didn't provide last week?

[07:47] Sara Weber: right, we still need architecture diagrams with KMS calls annotated, a list of who has HSM access, and proof that logs can't be altered during fallback. Also metadata retention policy.

[07:59] Maya Chen: we'll produce an updated security pack. Diego, include the control plane call-flow and the audit log sample.

[08:05] Diego Ramos: yes. Also note that our private deployment supports customer-managed KMS — if you want HSM retention >90 days we can give options.

[08:13] Priya Singh: for now we'll stick to existing HSM with Redwood-managed rotation, but send options.

[08:18] Speaker 2: minor item — someone asked about competitor notes, why not just use Vertex?

[08:24] Maya Chen: short answer, Vertex is fine but doesn't have our unified rollout and fallback playbook for private onprem with telemetry parity, which is why AsterMed chose Redwood. But we also respect your multi-cloud strategy.

[08:36] Liam O'Connor: ok thanks — one ops question: can Redwood's console emit alerts into our PagerDuty on these specific rollback triggers?

[08:45] Diego Ramos: absolutely. We'll map events to your PD service and can set escalation policies.

[08:50] Tomáš Novak: good — for the pcap I'll annotate which PD alerts corresponded to flaps.

[08:58] Maya Chen: all right, let's capture the definitive next steps — Diego, can you list the artifacts you'll deliver by Friday?

[09:05] Diego Ramos: sure: 1) kernel 2.4 canary runbook and instrumentation (including token-level sampling) 2) updated logging path and sample logs 3) audit diagram + KMS callflow 4) an annotated rollback test plan. I'll push to the secure share and ping Priya.

[09:20] Priya Singh: I'll share VPC peering config, the BGP adjacency history, and the MTU topology map. Expect that tonight.

[09:28] Sara Weber: I'll confirm the SOC2 list and schedule a 30-min security deep-dive for next week.

[09:34] Maya Chen: perfect. Recap: run a 3-hour synthetic then 12-hour soak on 2 canary nodes, collect pcaps and logs, toggle batching for isolated runs, and convene security call.

[09:45] Speaker 1: any blockers?

[09:48] Priya Singh: main blocker is time window for soak — we'll need to align with a low-traffic period; otherwise we can do an overnight soak starting 00:00 local.

[09:55] Liam O'Connor: also team availability for rollback; ops will be on-call tomorrow morning.

[09:59] Diego Ramos: Redwood will be on standby for canary window.

[10:03] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. I'll send minutes and the checklist. Meeting adjourned.
